## 1. Load the processed data

```{r load}
# Open the project's .Rproj file before running chunks.
# Install psych once in the Console if needed: install.packages("psych")

# install.packages("psych")
library("psych")

h1Data <- read.csv("data/processed_data/practice_h1.csv")
h2Data <- read.csv("data/processed_data/practice_h2.csv")

```

## 2. Look at the distribution first

```{r histogram}
# A histogram groups numerical values into intervals (bins).
# Bar height shows how many observations fall in each interval.
# Start by looking at the distribution before calculating summary statistics.
hist(h1Data$gender_equa,
     main="Distribution of Attitude about gender",
     xlab="Attitude about gender (1-7)")
hist(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1,
     main="Willingness to marry without love by intensity of love feelings",
     xlab="Magnitude of Willingness  (1-100)")
```

## 3. One statistic at a time

```{r individual_statistics}
# Mean: add the scores and divide by the number of observed responses.
mean(h1Data$gender_equa, na.rm=TRUE)
# Median: the middle score after sorting the responses.
median(h1Data$gender_equa, na.rm=TRUE)

# Table: count how many people are in each category.
table(h1Data$gender_equa, useNA = "ifany")
# Range: return the minimum and maximum, rather than their difference.
range(h1Data$gender_equa, na.rm=TRUE)
# IQR: the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile.
IQR(h1Data$gender_equa, na.rm=TRUE)
```

## 4. Standardize a variable

```{r standardize}
# scale() uses z = (original score - mean) / standard deviation by default.
# Keep the original commitment scores and store the standardized values separately.
# scale() returns a matrix; as.numeric() makes a simple numeric column.
h1Data$gender_equa_z <- scale(h1Data$gender_equa)

# Standardized scores have mean approximately 0 and standard deviation 1.
mean(h1Data$gender_equa_z, na.rm=TRUE)
sd(h1Data$gender_equa_z,  na.rm=TRUE)
```

## 5. Covariance and correlation

```{r association}
# Covariance describes whether two variables tend to move together.
# Positive: higher values tend to occur together. Negative: higher values tend to accompany lower values.
# Its size depends on the units and is not restricted to -1 through 1.
cov(h2Data$Love_how_much_1, h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1, use = "complete.obs")

# Select numerical variables only; do not include participant IDs or category codes.
corData <- h2Data[, c("Love_how_much_1","Love_would_you_marry_1")]

# A correlation matrix gives the correlation for each pair of columns.
# The diagonal is 1 because each variable is correlated with itself.
cor(corData, use="complete.obs")
```

## 6. Several statistics at once

```{r combined_summaries}
# summary() reports minimum, quartiles, median, mean, maximum, and missing counts when present.
summary(corData)
# psych::describe() reports n, mean, SD, median, minimum, maximum, range width (max minus min), skewness, kurtosis, and other summaries.
# However it does not report every statistic above: compute IQR, cov(), and cor() separately.
psych::describe(corData)

```
